paras: The bombing of the Jackson home on East 48th Street was an attack in Chicago on a house occupied by a Black couple, Mr. and Mrs. J. Jackson, by men who threw a bomb from a passing car shortly after midnight on a Sunday in early August 1920. The bomb broke windows but injured no one, and the bombers escaped. Two Chicago Black weeklies treated it as part of a series of bombings and faulted the authorities.

The house, at 440 E. 48th St., belonged to a Mrs. Brinkley of the South, and the Jacksons had moved in the Tuesday before. Neighborhood property owners had hired J. D. Hardiman, a retired army sergeant, as a watchman several weeks earlier.

Hardiman told the Chicago Whip that while patrolling the alley he saw a Ford touring car cruising along 48th Place, whose occupants threw an object that landed on the parkway, and that he fired several shots as the car sped off. The object was a bomb, and its explosion broke windows along 48th Place. The Chicago Defender said the bomb was thrown by "two white men" in an automobile.

According to the Defender, police tried to arrest the watchman, whom it called Joseph Harding, on a charge of assault with weapons, released him after bystanders objected, and let the driver of a suspected car leave without questioning. No report of an arrest of the bombers appears in the coverage.

No white-press report was found; both accounts appeared on August 14, 1920. The Whip headlined "Hoodlums' Bomb Does More Damage to White Than to Colored Homes," called the bombers "American reds," and said Cook county could convict William Bross Lloyd but not these "reds" who were "endangering lives." The Defender's headline, "Score Detectives in Bomb Plot," made police conduct its story.

Hardiman told the Whip he believed he hit somebody, while the Defender said his shots missed. The Whip said the white-occupied houses opposite suffered more than the target, while the Defender put damage to the Jackson home at several hundred dollars.

bases: A bomb was thrown from a passing automobile at a house occupied by a Black couple and exploded, breaking windows (A1, A2, A3).

accounts.label: Watchman Hardiman's statement (Chicago Whip)
accounts.gist: While patrolling the alley he saw a Ford touring car cruising 48th Pl.; its occupants threw an object that fell on the parkway, and he fired several shots at the speeding car and believes he hit someone.

accounts.label: Chicago Defender
accounts.gist: Two white men in an automobile hurled the bomb; the watchman's shots missed, police tried to arrest him instead, and they let a suspected driver leave; damage was several hundred dollars.

framing.detail: The Whip's headline 'Hoodlums' Bomb Does More Damage to White Than to Colored Homes' and its 'American reds' language cast the bombers as property destroyers whom the Cook county prosecutor would not pursue.
The Defender's headline 'Score Detectives in Bomb Plot / Officers Allow Bombers to Escape, but Nab Night-' made police conduct the story.

Not a mob: two white men in an automobile (Defender), occupants of a Ford touring car (Whip).
Two unidentified white men in an automobile.
'Sunday night at 12:30 A. M.' before August 14: August 8 or the early hours of August 9; exact calendar date not stated.
